content: The treatment of maize flour with lime, which converts niacin into a biologically available form, along with the inclusion of beans, groundnuts, or fortified cereals in daily diets, significantly increases the total intake of available niacin. This dietary modification effectively prevents the development of pellagra. Anemia is highly prevalent among refugee and displaced populations, as evidenced by limited publications and unpublished data from CDC assessments. A 1990 survey of Palestinian refugees in Syria, Jordan, and the West Bank revealed anemia prevalence rates of 50% to 70% among infants and young children. Among nonpregnant and pregnant women, anemia prevalence ranged from 25% to 50%, while the male population exhibited a lower prevalence. In this study, anemia was defined as a hemoglobin concentration of less than 11 g/dL in children and less than 12 g/dL in nonpregnant women, with a threshold of 10 g/dL during the second trimester of pregnancy. These findings suggest that iron deficiency, which disproportionately affects women and children, was the primary cause of anemia in this population. A 1987 study among refugees in Somalia reported anemia prevalence rates of 44% to 71% among pregnant women, with even higher rates observed in women in the third trimester of pregnancy. The hemoglobin cutoff in this study was 10 g/dL; using the WHO cutoff of 11 g/dL, the prevalence would have been even higher. Among children aged 9 to 36 months, 59% to 90% had hemoglobin levels below the 10 g/dL threshold. The inadequacy of the general food ration was identified as the major factor contributing to iron deficiency anemia in this population. In a 1990 study, the anemia prevalence rate was 13% among children under five years of age in an Ethiopian camp for Somali refugees (unpublished data from Save the Children Fund UK). In addition to dietary iron deficiency, the high incidence of malaria in many refugee populations likely contributes to the elevated prevalence of anemia in children. While the high prevalence of anemia in some refugee populations may not be significantly greater than that in local non-refugee populations, the latter group has been poorly documented. Nevertheless, anemia remains an important preventable risk factor for high mortality in refugee populations. Severe anemia, defined as hemoglobin levels below 5 g/dL, is often associated with high mortality rates, particularly among young children and pregnant women during the peripartum period. Thiamine deficiency, or beriberi, has been reported in several refugee populations reliant on rice-based food rations, such as in Thailand (1980) and Guinea (1990). Data on iodine deficiency in displaced populations are scarce, but anecdotal evidence suggests that iodine deficiency, indicated by the presence of goiter, has been a problem in some camps in Pakistan and Ethiopia. Communicable diseases, including measles, diarrheal diseases, acute respiratory infections (ARIs), and, in some cases, malaria, are the primary causes of morbidity and mortality among refugee and displaced populations. Densely populated camps with poor sanitation, inadequate clean water supplies, and substandard housing contribute to the rapid spread of disease. The interaction between malnutrition and infection, particularly among young children, exacerbates the high rates of morbidity and mortality from communicable diseases. Measles outbreaks in refugee camps have been common and have caused significant mortality. Low immunization coverage, combined with high rates of undernutrition and vitamin A deficiency, has played a critical role in the spread of measles and the associated mortality in some camps. Measles has been one of the leading causes of death among children in refugee camps and has contributed to high malnutrition rates among survivors. Measles infection can lead to or worsen vitamin A deficiency, compromising immunity and increasing susceptibility to xerophthalmia, blindness, and premature death. In early 1985, a measles outbreak in an eastern Sudan camp resulted in a crude measles-specific death rate of 13 per 1,000 per month. Among children under five years of age, the measles-specific death rate was 30 per 1,000 per month. Over 2,000 measles-related deaths were reported in this camp between February and May 1985. The case fatality rate (CFR) during this outbreak was reported to be 33%, though mild cases may have been underreported. Large numbers of measles deaths have also been reported in camps in Somalia, Bangladesh, Sudan, and Ethiopia. Mass immunization campaigns have been effective in reducing measles morbidity and mortality rates in camps in both Somalia and Thailand.
